question: How many zeros does \(f(x) = \cos(\log x)\) have on the interval \(0 \lt x \lt 1?\)
solution:
The interval \((0,1)\) is bounded, but its logarithms fill an entire unbounded half-line. This allows infinitely many cosine zeros to occur.

Write \(\log=\log_b\), where \(b>0\) and \(b\ne1\). In radians, cosine vanishes exactly when
\[
t=\frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
For the usual case \(b>1\), the condition \(0<x<1\) is equivalent to \(\log_bx<0\). The negative cosine-zero angles are exactly \(-\pi/2-n\pi\), where \(n=0,1,2,\ldots\). Consequently, all the zeros in the requested interval are
\[
x_n=b^{-\pi/2-n\pi},\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.
\]
Every one lies strictly between 0 and 1. Distinct indices give distinct exponents and hence distinct inputs, because the exponential function is one-to-one.

If \(0<b<1\), logarithms of inputs in \((0,1)\) are positive instead. The same argument gives the distinct zeros \(x_n=b^{\pi/2+n\pi}\), again all in \((0,1)\).

Thus there are \(\boxed{\text{infinitely many}}\) zeros, choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
